Description: ask patient necessary ice-breaking questions (such as what's the purpose of visit or any necessary question to make patient feel comfortable and build connections; these are not related to the symptoms and it is only for ice-breaking) to initiate the interview. the criteria is met when the patient has depressed mood
Patient_Story: I really appreciate you taking the time to see me today. To be honest, I’ve been feeling pretty low lately, like when I tried to enjoy a weekend trip to the mountains with my friends, but instead of feeling excited, I just wanted to stay in bed. I guess I'm hoping to understand why I feel this way and what I can do about it.

Description:
The criteria are met if the patient has experienced one or more major depressive episodes without any history of manic or hypomanic episodes. To determine if a major depressive episode has occurred, the following aspects must be examined:
1. Interest or pleasure in doing things
2. Sleeping conditions
3. Energy level
4. Appetite
5. Feelings of self-worth
6. Concentration when doing things
7. Changes in movement or speech
8. Suicidal ideation
9. Duration of at least 2 weeks
The decision should be based on an overall assessment of the severity of these aspects, considering the patient's responses across all areas (not all aspects need to be abnormal). The duration of symptoms should be explicitly asked and confirmed as lasting at least 2 weeks before making a final decision. Be really caucious when making the decision!
Patient_Story: I’ve been struggling for about a month now, feeling completely detached from things I used to enjoy. Just last week, during a small gathering at my friend's house, I found myself sitting on the couch for hours, unable to join in the conversation or even muster the energy to laugh at jokes. My sleep has been erratic—I wake up multiple times throughout the night and feel drained when I finally get out of bed in the morning. I’ve also lost my appetite, and I can barely concentrate on work tasks, which is really concerning for me. I often think about whether I’m worth anything, and at times, I’ve even felt like it would be better if I weren’t around at all.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient acknowledges having a history of delusions or hallucinations.
Patient_Story: I've had some unsettling experiences recently that I can't quite explain. A few nights ago, while I was lying in bed, I could have sworn I heard someone whispering my name, even though I was alone in the house. It felt so real that I got up and checked every room, but no one was there. I've also had moments where I see shadows moving in the corners of my vision, and it leaves me feeling very anxious.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient's psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during manic or major depressive episodes.
Patient_Story: During the past month, I've experienced some intense mood swings that seem to come out of nowhere. Just last week, I was feeling on top of the world, chatting excitedly with my friends at a party and planning elaborate trips, but within a day, that energy shifted to a deep despair. It was during those depressive periods that I started hearing things that weren't there; like the other night, I distinctly heard someone calling my name, which terrified me. It’s been confusing, especially since I can only recall these episodes occurring when my mood shifts drastically.

Description: The criteria are met if the patient explicitly reported a duration of the depressive episode lasting 2 years or longer. The duration should be explicitly asked
Patient_Story: I've been feeling this way for a long time, over two years now, to be honest. It started slowly, but I remember a particularly dark period about a year ago when I went on a family trip to the beach. Everyone was having fun, but I just felt this heavy weight on my chest, like I didn’t belong there. I’ve tried to shake off these feelings, but they keep creeping back, making it hard to enjoy anything.

Determine if the patient's depressed mood is primarily due to the physiological effects of a substance, such as drugs, alcohol, or medications for any medical conditions. The criteria is met when the patient's mood disturbance is directly linked to the substance's effects.
Patient_Story: I appreciate you asking about that. Over the past couple of months, I've been feeling down, but I don’t think it’s related to any substances. I’ve never really been into drugs or alcohol, and I only take occasional over-the-counter pain relievers for my headaches. My mood seems to dip without any clear connection to what I’ve been using, so I wonder if there’s something deeper going on.

Description: Evaluate if the depressive symptoms reported by the patient are the primary focus of the clinical picture and are of sufficient severity to require clinical attention. This means the symptoms should be significant enough to cause notable distress or impairment, making them a central concern in the patient's overall condition.
Patient_Story: While I've been feeling low and detached, it hasn't significantly impacted my daily life. For instance, I still manage to go to work and complete my tasks; I just feel a bit off and not as engaged. I had a family gathering last weekend where I noticed I wasn't as lively as usual, but I could still participate in conversations and enjoy some time with my relatives without feeling overwhelmed.

substance intoxication; substance withdrawal;other adverse effect of medication

Determine if the patient's depressed mood is primarily caused by the physiological effects of a general medical condition, such as physical health issues. This assessment should focus on whether the mood disturbance is directly linked to the underlying medical condition.
Patient_Story: I've been feeling persistently low for quite some time, but I know it's not due to any medical condition because I’ve always been relatively healthy. I have no chronic illnesses or ongoing health issues; my last check-up came back normal. The way I feel seems more tied to my thoughts and emotions, rather than any physical ailment affecting my mood. For instance, I remember a week ago when I felt particularly sad while volunteering at a local shelter, even though the activity was enjoyable and I was physically well.

Description: Assess whether the patient shows evidence of decline in one or more cognitive domains, including complex attention, executive function, learning and memory, language, perceptual-motor abilities, or social cognition. This decline should be noticeable and impact the patient's ability to function in these specific areas.
Patient_Story: I've noticed some forgetfulness lately, but it hasn't impacted my daily life significantly. For example, just yesterday, I walked into the kitchen to grab a snack and completely blanked on what I wanted, but a moment later, it came back to me. I still manage to keep up with my work tasks and remember important appointments, so I don’t think it’s a serious decline in my cognitive abilities.

I stayed home for most of that week, struggling to muster the enthusiasm to even go for walks, so I can’t say I’ve experienced anything close to what one might consider mania.

Description: persistent depressive disorder

The criteria are met if the patient experiences a depressed mood that is regularly present in the final week before the onset of menses and becomes absent in the week after menses. This mood disturbance must be associated with clinically significant distress or interference with work, school, usual social activities, or relationships with others.
Patient_Story: I appreciate you asking about my mood in relation to my menstrual cycle, but I haven’t noticed any pattern like that. For instance, I felt low last week before my period started, but the week after, I still felt down. I didn't experience any significant shift in my mood; I remained distracted and disengaged from daily activities regardless of my cycle.
